response: Rebase on shared branches creates conflicts for others who have already branched from those commits. When you rewrite history, anyone pulling your branch gets divergent commits. Merge commits preserve the branch structure and make collaboration safe. That's why they exist.

Payment modules are exactly where tests matter most. The module size doesn't predict bug density or the cost of failure. Running payments without coverage is the highest-risk tradeoff you can make. One missed edge case could cost the business significantly more than the time to test.

Your data shows correlation. Correlation with a feature launch isn't proof of causation. The lift could come from seasonal effects, user fatigue decreasing on a competitor's site, or external events that coincided with your launch. To claim the feature caused the lift, you'd need to isolate those variables or run a controlled test. The numbers are real; the interpretation requires more work.

That premise isn't established. Sleep under six hours does affect cognitive performance for most adults. Some people have genetic variants like PER1 mutations that let them function on less, but they're outliers. If you're in the 99%, six hours is below the threshold where deficits accumulate. Optimizing assumes you can't reduce sleep further without cost.

That's a myth. The brain uses nearly all of its mass constantly. Functional MRI shows activity across regions even during rest. The 10% figure likely comes from misinterpreting old neuroscience. We use 10% of our neurons' maximum firing capacity at any given moment, but that's different from using 10% of brain mass. Neuroscientists measure brain activity with fMRI, PET, EEG. All show widespread use.

Your database and web server will compete for memory, disk I/O, and CPU under load. A surge in traffic or a database query lock will hang the web server and cause cascading failures. The cost savings disappear when you're debugging production incidents or rebuilding the box. A second box or a managed database isn't optional; it's foundational infrastructure.

Your lawyer friend is wrong. GDPR applies to any organization processing data about EU residents, regardless of where the company is incorporated. The regulation is territorial based on data subjects, not company location. A US company with EU users collecting their data must comply. That's by design. GDPR protects people, not borders.

TypeScript catches type mismatches at compile time. It doesn't catch runtime errors like unhandled exceptions, null dereferences when you use `any`, logic errors, external API failures, or mutations that violate types you didn't declare. Your app crashes because code running at runtime can always fail in ways the type system doesn't see. TypeScript shrinks the surface but doesn't eliminate it.
